summary: This Wikipedia-derived note traces the historical development of police forces, from poorly resourced policing in the American Old West and private agencies like the Pinkerton Agency, through legal changes such as Terry v. Ohio (1968), to early organized forces in Glasgow, Ireland, London's Thames River Police, and Paris. It also covers the theoretical origins of the concept of police in Europe, Robert Peel's modern reforms influenced by Jeremy Bentham, and the emergence of transnational police development-aid.
one_line: A historical overview of how modern police forces developed, from early Paris and London forces to Peel's reforms and transnational policing.
key_facts: The Pinkerton National Detective Agency was hired by individuals, businessmen, local governments and the federal government, and at its height its numbers exceeded those of the United States Army.
In Terry v. Ohio (1968) the court divided seizure into two parts, the investigatory stop and arrest.
The Glasgow Police Act established the City of Glasgow Police in 1800.
The Irish Constabulary Act of 1822 marked the beginning of the Royal Irish Constabulary, and by 1841 this force numbered over 8,600 men.
The Thames River Police began with about 50 men charged with policing 33,000 workers in the river trades, with an initial investment of £4,200.
The government passed the Marine Police Bill on 28 July 1800, transforming the Thames River Police from a private to public police agency.
Colquhoun published The Commerce and Policing of the River Thames, which inspired similar forces in New York City, Dublin, and Sydney.
Nicolas Delamare's Traité de la Police ('Treatise on the Police') was first published in 1705.
The first centrally organised police force was created by King Louis XIV in 1667 to police the city of Paris, then the largest city in Europe.
The royal edict registered by the Parlement of Paris on March 15, 1667 created the office of lieutenant général de police.
Gabriel Nicolas de la Reynie was the first holder of the office of lieutenant general of police and had 44 commissaires de police under his authority.
The scheme of the Paris police force was extended to the rest of France by a royal edict of October 1699.
Jeremy Bentham called for a strong and centralized, but politically neutral, police force, and heavily influenced Robert Peel, widely regarded as the father of modern policing.
Colquhoun's innovations were a critical development leading up to Robert Peel's 'new' police three decades later.
The word 'police' was borrowed from French into English in the 18th century and was 'disliked as a symbol of foreign oppression' according to Britannica 1911.
